notes.meaning: Ezekiel was sitting at home in Babylon with the exiled leaders of Judah gathered before him. While they were waiting to hear a message, the power of the Lord came strongly upon the prophet. This moment began a whole new set of visions about Jerusalem and why it would be destroyed.

Ezekiel looked up and saw a glowing figure shaped like a man. From the waist down, the figure burned like blazing fire, and from the waist up, He shone like gleaming amber metal. The fire showed God's fierce anger against sin, while the brightness revealed His majestic holiness.

The divine figure reached out what looked like a hand and lifted Ezekiel up by the hair of his head. In this vision, the Holy Spirit carried him between earth and heaven all the way to the temple in Jerusalem. At the north gate of the inner court, Ezekiel saw a repulsive idol that provoked God's holy jealousy.

Right next to that shameful statue, Ezekiel saw the dazzling glory of the God of Israel. It was the very same glorious presence he had seen earlier by the river in Babylon. The pure beauty of the true God stood in sharp contrast to the ugly, lifeless idol set up in His home.

God told the prophet to look north toward the entrance of the altar gate, and there Ezekiel saw the idol of jealousy in plain view. Setting an idol right next to the altar where sacrifices were made was an open insult to the Lord. It showed how bold and rebellious the leaders had become.

God asked Ezekiel if he saw the terrible sins Israel was practicing right inside the sacred temple grounds. These evil acts were so offensive that they were driving the holy Lord away from His own sanctuary. Even so, God warned the prophet that he would soon witness even worse abominations.

The Lord brought Ezekiel to the entrance of the temple court, where the prophet spotted a hole in the wall. This opening led into hidden rooms that were kept out of public sight. God was preparing to expose the wicked things the leaders were trying to keep secret.

God told Ezekiel to dig through the wall, and when he did, he uncovered a hidden doorway. Ezekiel followed the command and prepared to enter the private chamber. God was showing him that no matter how well people hide their wrongdoing, He uncovers every secret corner.

The Lord told Ezekiel to step inside and see the terrible sins taking place in the dark. God wanted His prophet to look directly at the corruption so there would be no doubt about Judah's guilt. Seeing this explained why God's coming judgment was completely fair.

Ezekiel stepped inside and saw walls covered with carved pictures of crawling bugs, unclean beasts, and idols. These images came from Egyptian animal worship, which God's law strictly forbade. Instead of honoring their living Creator, the leaders were bowing down to drawings of low reptiles.

Standing in front of these carved images were seventy elders of Israel, with Jaazaniah son of Shaphan standing among them. Every man held a small pan called a censer, sending up thick clouds of sweet-smelling incense to the false gods. The very leaders who were supposed to teach the people to follow God were instead leading the way into idolatry.

God pointed out that these elders practiced their idolatry in the dark, each at his own hidden shrine. The elders told themselves that the Lord could not see them and had abandoned their land. They mistakenly thought that because God had been patient, He was blind to their wickedness.

The Lord told Ezekiel to look again, warning him that he would see even greater abominations. God was peeling back the layers of Judah's rebellion step by step. Each new scene showed false worship reaching deeper into sacred places.

God brought Ezekiel to the north gate of the Lord's house, where he found women sitting and weeping for the false god Tammuz. Tammuz was a Babylonian fertility god who was believed to die every year and need ritual mourning to bring life back to nature. Instead of weeping over their own sins before the true God, these women were crying for a dead pagan myth.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe the annual mourning ritual for Tammuz later influenced church seasons like Lent and Easter, while other evangelicals reject any historical connection.

notes.meaning: God asked Ezekiel if he had taken in this heartbreaking scene, and told him he would witness things that were worse still. The prophet was being led closer and closer to the very center of the temple. The nearer they came to God's holy throne room, the more offensive the rebellion became.

The Lord brought Ezekiel into the temple's inner court, right between the entrance porch and the bronze altar. About twenty-five men, likely leading priests, stood with their backs deliberately turned toward God's temple as they faced east to bow to the rising sun. Turning their backs on God's house showed utter contempt for Him as they worshipped creation instead of the Creator.

God asked Ezekiel if Judah thought their awful sins were a small matter, especially since they had also filled the whole land with cruelty and injustice. Corrupt worship had led straight into evil treatment of their neighbors. On top of that, they held branches to their noses, an insulting gesture that showed open mockery of God.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some Catholic translations follow an ancient scribal reading where the phrase means putting an offensive branch to God's own nose rather than their own.

notes.meaning: Because the leaders and people showed such stubborn rebellion, the Lord declared that He would bring down His full judgment without pity. Even when terror arrived and they screamed loudly for help, He would not listen to their cries. They had turned their backs on Him in times of peace, so He would not turn to rescue them in their ruin.
